title: Service chain isolation and fallback matrix — Dedicated / Hosted / Private
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a compact operational model for how a request traverses Redwood’s serving surface across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments, and how isolation contracts + fallback matrices should be specified and enforced. Goal is to produce a single, implementable policy table (service-chain + fallback) that platform code and SRE runbooks can reference.

High-level goals (non-exhaustive):
- Make the isolation boundary semantics explicit for each deployment mode (what can be shared, what is tenant-local).
- Define minimal, prioritized fallback behaviors by failure domain so apps degrade predictably.
- Surface decision points that must live in the control plane vs the data plane.
- Provide worked examples for multi-region failover and burst routing for Dedicated customers.

Key concepts / vocabulary (quick):
- Service chain: sequence of processing stages a request passes through (edge LB -> auth -> routing -> model pool -> postprocess).
- Isolation contract: a named guarantee describing resource separation (eg. data-plane isolation, KV cache visibility, audit log tenancy).
- Fallback matrix: ordered list of fallback targets/behaviors when a stage fails or violates SLO thresholds.
- Decision point: location (control plane, edge, or serving runtime) responsible for making a routing/fallback decision.
- Compatibility profile: lightweight descriptor that indicates which model variants/capacity tiers are interoperable for fallback.

Service chain model (simplified):
1. Edge LB (ingress) — initial auth, quick policy checks, geo/region affinity, preliminary rate-limit.
2. Control-plane policy lookup — resolve tenant routing policy (hosted/dedicated/private), model pins, allowed fallbacks.
3. Router (data-plane) — binds request to compute pool (dedicated pod, tenant-annotated hosted instance, private VPC endpoint).
4. Serving runtime — model execution (KV/cache use, quantization profile).
5. Postprocess + observability sink — cost attribution, tracing, SLO checks.

Isolation contracts (summary table, informal):
- Data-plane isolation:
  Hosted: tenant data may travel through shared GPUs and shared KV caches but must be encrypted in transit and logically segregated (prefix namespace) — stronger contract only for paid Dedicated/Private tiers.
  Dedicated: tenant-exclusive GPUs, KV caches pinned per-reservation; clear physical isolation guarantees.
  Private: full customer-managed network and control plane endpoints; data plane never leaves customer VPC unless explicitly enabled.

- Control-plane visibility:
  Hosted: control plane centrally manages policies and can see routing telemetry; customers get aggregated metrics and audit logs.
  Dedicated: control plane still schedules, but visibility of raw payloads is restricted; enhanced audit/logging for tenant operators.
  Private: customer runs control plane or uses private control plane with limited operator visibility by contract.

- Egress / outbound policies:
  Hosted: egress routes through Redwood-managed NATs; per-tenant egress controls exist but are coarse.
  Dedicated: can configure VPC peering or dedicated egress.
  Private: customer controls full egress and firewall rules.

Decision point breakdown (who decides what):
- AuthN/AuthZ: Edge (short-circuit) + control plane (policy resolution).
- Region affinity: Edge based on geo and latency SLO, control plane enforces permitted regions for tenant.
- Fallback selection: Control plane returns an ordered compatibility profile; data-plane router enforces immediate fallback when target pool is unavailable.
- Cache reuse: Serving runtime enforces KV visibility rules (local-only for dedicated/private; prefix-based for hosted).

Fallback matrix (operational priority list) — generic ordering by failure domain:
1) Local pool retry (fast, same machine/pod) — transient CPU/GPU hiccup / OOM mitigation.
2) Tenant-dedicated spare capacity (if reserved) — for Dedicated customers who have burst capacity configured.
3) Region-local Hosted fallback (for Hosted-only customers) — use compatible hosted model variant in same region.
4) Cross-region fallback (regional failover) — respects data locality policy and customer allowlist.
5) Lower-capacity model variant (quantized / smaller) — cost/quality tradeoff explicit in compatibility profile.
6) Fallback to synchronous cached response / cached prompt-prefix (if available) — last-resort for tail-latency control.
7) Error surface to client with explicit degradation code and recommended retry-after.

Notes on ordering rationale:
- Prefer in-region and tenant-local capacity to minimize data movement and latency.
- Prefer higher-quality variants first; lower-capacity variants are explicitly signaled to customers (via response header).
- Cross-region fallback must check Tenant egress/locality contract before routing.

Compatibility profile examples (illustrative):
- profile: redwood-gpt-large-compat
  allowed-fallbacks: [redwood-gpt-medium-quant, redwood-gpt-small-quant]
  quality-impact: medium -> low (explicit header: X-RW-Fallback-Quality)
  allowed-regions: [us-west-2, us-east-1]

- profile: private-customer-1-primary
  allowed-fallbacks: [private-customer-1-secondary]  # only private pools
  allowed-regions: [eu-west-1]
  cross-region-allowed: false

Operational examples (short):
1) Dedicated customer with reserved pool hits sudden 5x spike:
   - Router consults control plane for burst policy -> sends traffic to tenant-spare-capacity pool (step 2 fallback).
   - If spare exhausted, router tries same-region hosted-compatible model per contract (if allowed).
   - SRE runbook triggers capacity alert and auto-scale window.

2) Hosted tenant in us-east-1 experiences pod-level OOM during long-context request:
   - Fast local retry (same pod) with lower work quantum.
   - If OOM persists, router rebinds to different hosted pool in same region (step 3).
   - If region overloaded, consider cross-region fallback if tenant policy allows; otherwise return controlled degradation.

3) Private deployment (on-prem) partial network outage connecting to central control plane:
   - Local control plane mirrors previously-cached routing policy; data-plane continues serving on pinned pools.
   - If mirror stale beyond TTL -> block any fallback that would exit customer VPC (strict isolation contract).
   - Operator action: restore control plane sync; log and escalate with SRE.

Control plane vs data plane responsibilities (practical split):
- Control plane: policy authoring, compatibility profiles, region allowed lists, SLA thresholds that change fallback ordering, rollout windows.
- Data plane (router/runtime): fast enforcement of contract, local health checks, fail-open/fail-closed mechanics as per profile, immediate retries, cost attribution.

Implementation checklist (short actionable items):
- [ ] Define JSON schema for compatibility_profile and make it part of tenant config (include fallback order, allowed_regions, quality_penalty).
- [ ] Add response headers for any fallback used (X-RW-Fallback-Used, X-RW-Fallback-Quality).
- [ ] Router: implement in-memory per-tenant policy cache with TTL + stale-mode behavior for private deployments.
- [ ] Add a test harness that simulates the 7-step fallback matrix for each deployment mode.
- [ ] Update SLO runbooks to reflect new degradation codes and retry-after semantics.

Open questions / tradeoffs we should decide soon:
- Should Hosted tenants be allowed cross-region fallback by default? Pros: availability. Cons: data residency and latency; needs opt-out. Recommend default: opt-in for cross-region.
- How to represent soft vs hard isolation in a single contract? Suggest two fields: isolation_level (hard|soft) + allowed_shared_resources [list].
- For Dedicated customers, should we allow automatic spillover to hosted pools if tenant explicitly permits? Need legal/compliance sign-off.

Appendix: runbook snippets (placeholders)
- When routing returns 503 and fallback used: tag trace with fallback_type and notify #platform-routing with trace id.
- For Private control plane stale cache: if stale > TTL and attempt to fallback across egress boundary -> block and increment compliance metric.

References / pointers:
- PE-4123 (tenant routing policy schema)
- infra PR 578 (router policy cache implementation)
- Slack thread: #platform-routing / thread ZT-983 (multi-region fallback debate)

Notes to self: keep this intentionally prescriptive — platform code needs an exact ordering. This is a working doc, expect iterations.
